sections.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions

content.title: Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions
content.overview: This section provides a trauma-informed, practical guide to understanding the core purpose of myths and misconceptions and how it shapes physical, emotional, and relational safety in daily family life. Designed for parents, caregivers, and family support practitioners, it focuses on realistic, repeatable steps that strengthen safety, predictability, and connection.
content.psychoeducation: Why does myths and misconceptions matter in section 1? Children and families thrive on predictability, nervous-system safety, and attuned repair. When myths and misconceptions is practised consistently, stress responses decrease and relational trust grows. Why myths and misconceptions matters for child development.
learning_goals: Understand the purpose and value of myths and misconceptions. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions)
Identify common challenges and how to respond calmly. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions)
Practice simple, repeatable strategies that build confidence. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions)
Strengthen connection and emotional safety during difficult moments. (Foundations & Baseline Understanding: Myths and Misconceptions)
step_by_step: Pause & Ground: Notice your own breathing, body tension, and tone before addressing myths and misconceptions.
Observe Factually: Notice what is happening in the moment around myths and misconceptions without blame or judgement.
Connect & Validate: Acknowledge feelings and safety needs clearly and calmly.
Respond Simply: Choose one clear, age-appropriate action or boundary for myths and misconceptions.
Reflect & Repair: Review what worked, repair any rupture honestly, and record your next small step.
parent_scripts: "I can see this moment feels big right now. Let's slow down and take one step together with myths and misconceptions."
"Everyone is safe here. We can talk about what happened and work out the next step calmly."
"I noticed I was getting stressed. I'm taking a breath so I can listen properly."
"We don't have to get everything perfect today — we are practising myths and misconceptions one routine at a time."
practical_examples: Everyday Routine: Applying myths and misconceptions during a busy morning or bedtime transition by slowing down, offering two calm choices, and keeping tone steady.
Moment of Stress: When tension rises around myths and misconceptions, pausing for 10 seconds before speaking, validating feelings, and focusing on safety first.
Follow-Through & Review: Recording a factual note after practising myths and misconceptions to notice what helped the child settle and what support would help next time.
reflection_questions: What part of myths and misconceptions feels easiest for me?
What part feels hardest, and why?
How did my own childhood shape my reactions?
What is one small change I can try this week?
practice_ideas: Try a 2-minute grounding exercise before responding to your child.
Practice naming emotions using simple, non-judgemental language.
Role-play a challenging moment and rehearse a calm script.
Identify one routine where myths and misconceptions can be used daily.
content.closing_message: Progress in myths and misconceptions comes from small, consistent moments of safety, honesty, and repair — not perfection. Every time you pause, stay regulated, and choose a safer response, you build lasting trust.

content_variants.toddlers: For babies & toddlers (0–4): Focus on gentle tone, physical comfort, predictable routines, and simple 3-to-5 word reassurance while practising myths and misconceptions.
content_variants.school_age: For school-age children (5–11): Use clear explanations, visual routines, curiosity about their feelings, and collaborative problem-solving around myths and misconceptions.
content_variants.teens: For adolescents (12–18): Respect autonomy, listen without lecturing, agree on clear safety boundaries, and involve teens in decisions about myths and misconceptions.
content_variants.fatherhood: For fathers & male caregivers: Model calm accountability, steady emotional presence, and non-frightening leadership when practising myths and misconceptions.

red_flags: Immediate physical danger, threats, intimidation, or coercive control observed during myths and misconceptions.
A child shows fear, freezing, dissociation, or disclosure of harm related to myths and misconceptions.
An adult is unable to regulate or maintain safe supervision while attempting myths and misconceptions.
Signs of acute mental health crisis or substance intoxication affecting child safety.
when_to_escalate: Pause learning immediately if anyone is in danger and use verified emergency or crisis supports.
Follow jurisdiction-specific child protection and mandatory reporting obligations when harm is disclosed or suspected.
Engage a qualified supervisor, specialist DFV practitioner, or clinician when risk exceeds self-directed learning.

trauma_informed.clinical: Nervous-system lens for myths and misconceptions: Recognises fight, flight, freeze, and fawn survival responses, window of tolerance, and the need for co-regulation before cognitive problem-solving.
trauma_informed.relational: Attachment lens for myths and misconceptions: Prioritises connection before correction, attunement to cues, shame-free accountability, and timely repair after ruptures.
trauma_informed.justice: Fairness & cultural lens for myths and misconceptions: Respects cultural strengths, kinship networks, neurodiversity, disability access, and structural barriers without equating poverty with neglect.
trauma_informed.fatherhood: Accountable fatherhood lens for myths and misconceptions: Replaces control or withdrawal with steady, reliable care, honest repair, and child-centred safety.

sections.simplified_parent_version:
What myths and misconceptions means:
Myths and Misconceptions is about keeping daily life safe, calm, and predictable so your child feels supported and understood.

How to practise it:
1. Pause and take one slow breath first.
2. Notice what your child needs right now.
3. Use a calm voice and one clear step.
4. Repair kindly if things go off track.
